tasks.title: Parsing git grep -n output
tasks.statement: Write a function grep_matches(output): output is the text printed by git grep -n (possibly with -W or -p, and with --heading and --break). Return a list of [path, line_number, text] for MATCH lines only, in output order. Line format: without --heading every line starts with the path and a separator, then the line number, the same separator and the text. The separator is ':' for a matching line, '-' for a context line (-W, -A, -B, -C) and '=' for a function-name line (-p, -W). The path ends at the first place where a separator, a number and the same separator follow one another. With --heading the file name is printed once on its own line, and then come lines 'number:text' (match), 'number-text' (context) and 'number=text' (function). The line '--' separates groups, an empty line (--break) separates files, and a line 'Binary file PATH matches' is ignored. The text of a match may itself contain colons and numbers. Return the line number as an integer. Paths in the tests contain no fragments like ':number:', '-number-' or '=number='.
tasks.hint: For a line without a heading a regular expression with a non-greedy path and a back-reference to the separator works: ^(.+?)([:=-])(\d+)\2(.*)$. When the file is given by a heading, parse the line as ^(\d+)([:=-])(.*)$.

tasks.title: Looking up a name in a tags file
tasks.statement: Write a function find_tag(tags, name, from_file, kind): tags is the text of a ctags (universal-ctags) tags file, name is an exact name, from_file is the file you search from or None, kind is a kind letter or None. Every line holds a name, a file and the rest, all separated by tabs. The rest is an address, then ';"', then fields separated by tabs. Lines starting with '!' are pseudo-tags: skip them. The address is either a number (a line number) or a pattern /^...$/ (inside the pattern '\/' means '/' and '\\' means '\'). The address ends at the LAST occurrence of ';"' in the line: the pattern itself may contain such characters. Fields: a field without a colon is the kind; 'kind:X' is the kind too; 'file:' (an empty value) marks a static symbol visible only in its own file; 'line:N' is the line number; 'struct:X', 'class:X', 'union:X', 'enum:X', 'function:X' give the scope; ignore other fields. Return a list of rows [file, line_number, kind, scope, pattern]: the number comes from the line field, otherwise from a numeric address, otherwise None; scope and pattern are None when absent; the pattern has no '/^' and '$/' frame. Take only tags with exactly this name; if kind is given, only that kind; static tags only if from_file equals their file or from_file is None. Order: by file, then by line number (count None as zero).
tasks.hint: rest.rfind(';"') separates the address from the fields. Split the line with name, file, rest = line.split('\t', 2); the fields are rest[idx+2:].split('\t') without empty ones.

tasks.title: Parsing git blame --porcelain
tasks.statement: Write a function parse_blame(text): text is the output of git blame --porcelain for one file. Format: before every group of lines from one commit comes a header '<40 hex> <original line> <final line> <number of lines in the group>'. The following lines of the same group have a shorter header: '<40 hex> <original line> <final line>'. The commit information (author, author-mail, author-time, summary, filename and others) is printed ONLY the first time a commit appears; later groups of the same commit do not repeat it. The file line itself follows the header and starts with a tab (strip the tab). Ignore unknown header lines (for example previous and boundary). Return a dictionary {'lines': [[final_line_number, first_8_chars_of_hash, author, text], ...] in file order, 'authors': [[author, line_count], ...]}; sort authors by line count descending, ties by name.
tasks.hint: Check for a leading tab first: that is file content and may hold anything. Remember the author by hash on first sight and reuse it for later groups.

tasks.title: Threads and stacks from gdb
tasks.statement: Write a function summarize_threads(text): text is the output of gdb -batch -ex 'thread apply all bt' for a process. gdb prints threads in descending order of number. A thread header is 'Thread N (DESCRIPTION):' where DESCRIPTION holds '(LWP number)' or 'process number' and possibly ends with the thread name in double quotes: 'Thread 2 (Thread 0x7f.. (LWP 4249) "CPU 0/KVM"):'. A frame line is '#N  ' + (address '0x... in ' - not always) + function + ' (' + arguments + ')' + (' at file:line' or ' from library' - not always). The arguments may contain nested parentheses and quoted strings, and a string may even contain ' at x.c:9'. The function may be '??'. Ignore lines that do not start with '#' and are not thread headers (local variables, '(More stack frames follow...)', warnings, '[New LWP ...]'). Return a list in ASCENDING thread number, one row per thread: [number, LWP, name_or_None, frame_0_function, frame_count, 'file:line' of the topmost frame that has ' at file:line', or None]. LWP is an integer (for 'process N' take N).
tasks.hint: Parsing a frame: strip '#N  ' and the optional '0x... in ', take the name up to the first ' (', then walk the characters counting parentheses and skipping quoted text to find the closing parenthesis of the arguments; the tail after it is ' at ...' or ' from ...'.

tasks.title: From perf script to folded stacks
tasks.statement: Write a function fold_perf_script(text) that turns perf script output into folded stacks for a flame graph (after stackcollapse-perf.pl). Samples are separated by an empty line; skip lines starting with '#'. A sample header is a line that does not start with a space: 'comm pid/tid [cpu] time: period event:' (the period may be absent, then it is 1; pid/tid may be just 'tid'). The comm may contain spaces, for example 'CPU 0/KVM'. The event is the last word before the colon at the end of the line. Count only samples of the event seen FIRST, skip the others. Then come frame lines, the DEEPEST frame first: 'address symbol (module)'. Strip the '+0x...' suffix from the symbol; replace the symbol '[unknown]' with '[module_file_name]' (the last path component of the module), and if the module is also '[unknown]' with '[unknown]'; replace ';' in a symbol with ':'. The result is a list of lines 'comm;root;...;leaf period', where spaces in comm are replaced by '_' and comm comes first, frames go from the root to the leaf, and the periods of equal stacks are added. Sort the lines as plain strings.
tasks.hint: Header: re.match(r'^(\S.*?)\s+(\d+)/*(\d+)*\s+', line), period and event: re.search(r':\s*(\d+)*\s+(\S+):\s*$', line). Frame: re.match(r'^\s*(\w+)\s*(.+) \((.*)\)', line). Frames are read leaf first, so insert each new one at the front of the list.

tasks.title: Self and Children from folded stacks
tasks.statement: Write a function profile(lines): lines is a list of folded stacks 'root;...;leaf number', as printed by stackcollapse-perf.pl. The number is the sample weight, frame names contain no spaces. Skip empty lines. For every function compute self - the weight of stacks where it is the LEAF, and children (the Children column of perf report, that is inclusive time) - the weight of stacks where it appears AT LEAST ONCE (recursion counts once per stack). Return a list of rows [function, self, inclusive] sorted by inclusive descending, then by self descending, then by name.
tasks.hint: rsplit(' ', 1) splits off the weight. For inclusive time walk over set(frames) of each stack.

tasks.title: Roles of the threads of a QEMU process
tasks.statement: Write a function classify_threads(ps_output, pid): ps_output is the output of 'ps -T -o tid,comm -p PID' (the first line is a header; every next line holds the thread id first and then the thread name comm, which may contain spaces), pid is the process id. QEMU thread names, checked against the QEMU 11.1 source: 'CPU <n>/KVM' and 'CPU <n>/TCG' - the thread of virtual CPU n; 'IO <id>' - an iothread with this id (including the monitor's 'IO mon_iothread'); 'worker' - a thread-pool worker; 'call_rcu' - the deferred-free thread; 'vhost-<number>' - a kernel vhost thread. The main thread is the one whose id equals pid, its name does not matter (it is the program name cut to 15 characters). Any other name is 'other'. Return a dictionary: {'main': main_tid_or_None, 'vcpus': [[number, tid], ...] ascending by number, 'iothreads': [[id, tid], ...] ascending by id as strings, 'workers': number of worker threads, 'rcu': tid_or_None, 'vhost': [tid, ...] ascending, 'other': [[tid, comm], ...] ascending by tid}. All tids are integers.
tasks.hint: Split a line with tid, _, comm = line.strip().partition(' '); comm.strip(). Check tid == pid first, then regular expressions: ^CPU (\d+)/(KVM|TCG)$, ^IO (.+)$, ^vhost-\d+$.

tasks.title: The shortest path from an entry point to a function
tasks.statement: Write a function find_path(graph, entries, goal): graph is a dictionary 'function -> list of functions it calls' (what you collect with git grep and gdb bt), entries is a list of possible entry points (for example names from a thread's stack), goal is the target function. Return the SHORTEST path [entry, ..., goal] along the edges of the graph. If several shortest paths exist, return the lexicographically smallest one (lists of names compare element by element). If goal equals an entry, the path is that single name. If there is no path, return []. Functions that are not keys of the graph call nothing. The graph has cycles. An entry may be missing from the graph - then it leads nowhere (but may still be the goal).
tasks.hint: A reverse breadth-first search from goal gives distances dist to the goal. Then walk forward: choose the entry with the smallest dist (ties - the smaller name), and at every step take the smallest successor whose dist is one less.

tasks.title: A QTAILQ queue and container_of by hand
tasks.statement: This is a source-reading exercise: in QEMU 11.1 the file include/qemu/queue.h defines the QTAILQ queue and include/qemu/compiler.h defines the container_of macro. Open them in the project and rewrite the macros you need as plain functions for one type. Given: struct Job with a field entry - a union of the pointer tqe_next and the link QTailQLink tqe_circ; union JobQ is the queue head. The tql_prev link of an element points to the link of the PREVIOUS element (for the first one - to the head's link), the head's link points to the link of the last element, and tql_next holds a pointer to the element itself. Write: the macro container_of(ptr, type, member) (from a pointer to a field return a pointer to the struct; the member may be nested, for example entry.tqe_circ); jobq_init, jobq_insert_tail and jobq_remove after QTAILQ_INIT, QTAILQ_INSERT_TAIL and QTAILQ_REMOVE; jobq_last - the last element through container_of from q->tqh_circ.tql_prev; jobq_prev - like QTAILQ_PREV (the result is NULL for the first element). A removed element must get tql_prev and tqe_next equal to NULL (this is how QTAILQ_IN_USE tells that an element is not queued). The macro must be used in the program at least twice.
tasks.hint: For an empty queue tqh_circ.tql_prev points to the head itself. Insert at the tail: the new element's link gets the old tqh_circ.tql_prev, then the tql_next of that link (for an empty queue - tqh_first) becomes the new element, then tqh_circ.tql_prev points to the new link. Removal is the mirror operation.

tasks.title: Thread names as in QEMU: CPU n/KVM
tasks.statement: From this chapter you know that QEMU names its threads: 'CPU %d/KVM' for a virtual CPU (accel/kvm/kvm-accel-ops.c) and 'IO <id>' for an iothread, and qemu_thread_create sets the name with pthread_setname_np (util/qemu-thread-posix.c; QEMU ignores the error because the name is only for debugging). This is a real call to the kernel and there is no model: write three functions. thread_set_name(name) - name the calling thread with pthread_setname_np(pthread_self(), name) and return 0 or the error number (per man7.org the name is limited to 16 bytes including the terminator, a longer one gives ERANGE). vcpu_thread_name(buf, size, index) - write 'CPU <index>/KVM' and return 0 only if the string fits the buffer whole and is at most 15 characters; otherwise return -1 and make buf an empty string. other_thread_names(names, max) - what 'ps -T' does: walk the directory /proc/self/task, for every numeric directory name except the main thread id (getpid()) read /proc/self/task/<tid>/comm and return the number of names (without the newline).
tasks.hint: pthread_setname_np returns the error number, not -1 with errno. snprintf returns the length that would have been written without truncation: compare it with size and with 15. Read the directory with opendir/readdir, the comm file with fopen/fgets, and strip the newline with strcspn.
